$comment: The top-level entry points every runtime must present.
`formatter-options.json` pins what the formatters ACCEPT and
`formatter-helpers.json` pins what a CUSTOM formatter can be built from.
This pins the functions a caller reaches FIRST, which nothing else checked:
Rust had `highlight_events` and JavaScript had `highlightEvents` while Elixir
could only get the event stream inside a custom formatter's `render/3`
(#1543). Nothing failed, because a function one runtime lacks raises no error
where it does exist.
`name` is the canonical snake_case capability. Rust and Elixir spell it
verbatim, JavaScript camelCases it. `spelling` records the exceptions. A
spelling may be a list where a runtime splits one capability across several
functions, and a spelling containing `::` or `.` names a home outside the
scanned surface.
The scanned surface is the module a caller reaches first, and it is what the
reverse direction checks:
- Rust: module-level `pub fn` in `crates/lumis/src/lib.rs` and
`crates/lumis/src/highlight.rs`. `#[doc(hidden)]` is not public.
- JavaScript: the value exports of `packages/javascript/lumis/src/index.ts`
and `index.browser.ts`. Types are erased, so only functions are seen.
- Elixir: the `Lumis` module's exported functions. `@doc false` is not
public.
A capability whose home is outside that surface -- `lumis::languages::guess`,
`Lumis.Languages.guess/2` -- is checked by being CALLED, not by the scan,
because the scan cannot see it. That is also why the manifest does not have
to classify everything in `lumis::themes` or `Lumis.Languages`.
Two things are deliberately out of scope. The CLI is not a runtime here: its
top level is a set of commands rather than functions, and
`formatter-options.json` already pins its flags. And there is no `deprecated`
section, unlike `formatter-helpers.json`: what is deprecated at this level is
an arity of a capability that is not going anywhere -- `Lumis.highlight/3`
with the language first -- and every check below is by name, so the section
would have nothing to hold.
There is no shared output contract here, unlike `formatter-helpers.json`.
What these functions return is already pinned elsewhere and by exact bytes:
`fixtures/conformance/*/fixture.json` for `highlight` and `highlight_events`,
`fixtures/language-guess-cases.json` and `fixtures/language-detection.json`
for `guess`, and `fixtures/conformance-languages` for the catalog. This file
answers the question those cannot: whether the function is there at all.
Adding an entry point means adding it here first, then watching the three
local implementations go red. `runtime_only` and `waived` are the two escape
hatches, both carry their reason, and both are checked, so neither can grow
quietly.

capabilities.name: highlight
capabilities.$comment: Source plus a formatter, in, rendered output out. The one call the README leads with in every runtime.

capabilities.name: highlight_events
capabilities.$comment: The nested open/close event stream, without a formatter. Elixir lacked this until #1543.

capabilities.name: highlight_iter
capabilities.$comment: Flat per-token iteration: text, language, range, scope, resolved style. Waived for Elixir below.

capabilities.name: guess
capabilities.$comment: Resolve a name, an alias or a path to a language, falling back to plain text.

capabilities.name: available_languages
capabilities.$comment: Every language in the catalog, with its aliases and extensions.

capabilities.name: available_themes
capabilities.$comment: Every built-in theme's name and appearance.

capabilities.name: language_info
capabilities.$comment: One language looked up by id or alias, without scanning the catalog.

$comment: Entry points one runtime publishes at the top level and the others should
not, because the boundary dictates it rather than taste. Each entry says
why, and the tests fail on a name here that the runtime no longer exports,
so the list cannot outlive its reasons.
"Only this runtime" is about the top level. Where another runtime has the
same capability somewhere else, the reason says where.

rust.write_highlight: Streams into a `&mut dyn Write`, so a large document never exists as one `String`. JavaScript builds strings and Elixir returns iodata the caller hands to Phoenix; neither has a writer to stream into.

javascript.createHighlighter: Splits async setup from synchronous rendering, because loading a parser is a promise here. Rust's `lumis::highlight::Highlighter` is a type rather than an entry point, and Elixir's NIF loads inside `highlight/2`, so neither has an async phase to split off.
javascript.loadLanguages: Warms the parser cache before the first render. Elixir has `Lumis.Languages.load/1` and `async_load/1`, and the CLI has `lumis install`, so this is only top-level here; Rust's grammars are compiled in by cargo feature, so it has nothing to load.
javascript.runtimeKind: Reports whether the Wasmtime addon or `web-tree-sitter` is highlighting. JavaScript alone ships both runtimes in one package; the CLI, Elixir and Rust each have exactly one, so there is nothing to ask.
javascript.withWasm: Attaches statically imported parser bytes to a language so a bundler can see them. Rust compiles grammars in, and the CLI and Elixir fetch and verify them at run time, so neither has a bundler to satisfy.
javascript.configureWasmResolver: Overrides where parser assets are fetched from. Elixir configures that with `config :lumis, :parser_dirs` and the CLI with its config file, neither of which is a function.
javascript.sanitizeThemeName: Already pinned for all three runtimes in `formatter-helpers.json` under `html`. JavaScript also re-exports it at the package root, where its themes are plain objects the caller names, so it is top-level only here.

elixir.default_options: The validated default keyword list. Options are a `NimbleOptions` schema here, so a caller can read the defaults back; Rust's are a typed builder's `Default` and JavaScript's an object literal, neither of which is a function.
elixir.validate_options!: Checks a keyword list against the same schema before `highlight/2` does, so a caller can fail early on user input. Rust's builder and JavaScript's types reject the same mistakes at compile time.

$comment: A canonical capability a runtime does not offer. Each entry carries its
reason and, where it is a gap rather than a boundary, the issue tracking
it. The tests fail on a waiver the runtime has since grown, so it can only
shrink.
Unlike `formatter-options.json` and `formatter-helpers.json`, whose tests
assert this section is empty, this one starts with an entry. It is the gap
#1544 was opened about.

elixir.highlight_iter: Not implemented. Rust has `highlight_iter/4` and JavaScript has `highlightIter`; Elixir has no flat per-token walk, only the nested stream from `highlight_events/3`. It is implementable on top of that, so this waiver is a gap and not a boundary, and dropping it is the point.
